q: A team keeps enlarging a network past the point where it can fit the training set exactly. Under double descent, what happens to test error beyond that interpolation threshold?
options: It rises and stays high, because a model that fits every training label has memorised all of the noise for good
It flattens at the threshold value, because the model has reached its maximum useful capacity
It can fall again, because gradient descent tends to pick smooth, small-norm fits among the many perfect ones
It drops straight to the noise floor, because over-parameterised models are unable to overfit at all
explanation: Test error peaks near the interpolation threshold — the size at which the model can first fit the training set exactly (for simple models, roughly parameters ≈ training examples) — and then falls again as the model grows (Belkin et al., 2019; Nakkiran et al., 2019). The leading explanation is implicit regularization: among the many perfect fits, gradient descent finds smooth, small-norm ones, so variance drops again. The decomposition bias² + variance + noise still holds; only the rule 'more parameters ⇒ more variance' breaks.

q: Bagging (random forest) and boosting (XGBoost) both combine trees. Which statement correctly describes what each mainly reduces?
options: Bagging averages deep, high-variance trees built in parallel to cut variance; boosting adds shallow trees in sequence, each fitting the remaining errors, to cut bias
Bagging adds weak learners one at a time to cut bias; boosting averages strong trees trained on independent bootstrap samples to cut variance
Both mainly cut variance by aggregation; the only real difference is whether the trees are trained in parallel or one after another
Bagging mainly removes outlier sensitivity through robust averaging; boosting mainly removes feature correlation through heavy subsampling
explanation: Averaging cancels variance but not bias, so a random forest averages deep, low-bias trees. Boosting removes bias step by step, so each step is a weak, shallow tree (depth 3–8; XGBoost's default is 6) fitted to the errors left so far; shrinkage and subsampling also curb its variance. That is why random forests use deep trees and boosting uses shallow ones.

q: A spam classifier scores 72% training accuracy and 70% validation accuracy, while careful human raters reach about 95%. If you collect 5× more training data and change nothing else, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Validation accuracy climbs sharply, because the bigger sample reveals patterns hidden in the small one
Little changes: the 23-point gap to the target is bias, and more data mainly reduces variance
The train–validation gap widens, because more data lets the model memorise finer training detail
Both numbers approach the 95% target, because more data removes bias and variance equally
explanation: Avoidable bias = target − training = 95 − 72 = 23 points; variance = training − validation = 2 points. That is high bias — the chapter's logistic regression on a few hand-made features. More data shrinks variance, not bias: a model that cannot represent the pattern keeps the same bias however much data it sees. Fix bias first with richer features (word n-grams, sender reputation) or a more flexible model such as gradient-boosted trees.

q: Adam starts with m₀ = 0 and v₀ = 0 (β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999). What would the very first update look like WITHOUT bias correction?
options: About 10× too small, because m₁ = 0.1·g₁ understates the gradient and nothing compensates for it
Exactly the learning rate α, because the zero starts in m and v cancel each other out
Zero, because both moment estimates are still sitting at their initial value on step one
About 3.16× too large, because v₁ = 0.001·g₁² is understated far more than m₁ = 0.1·g₁
explanation: Uncorrected, the step is α·m₁/√v₁ = α·0.1·g₁/√(0.001·g₁²) ≈ 3.16·α in the gradient's direction — too LARGE, because v is understated 1,000× and sits under a square root, while m is understated only 10×. Dividing by (1 − 0.9ᵗ) and (1 − 0.999ᵗ) makes the first step exactly ±α. The v correction fades slowly — its factor is still 10.5 at t = 100 and 1.58 at t = 1,000 — so bias correction matters for the first few thousand steps.

q: On ResNet-style image classifiers, well-tuned SGD with momentum often matched or beat Adam's test accuracy. Which explanation matches the current view?
options: SGD's unscaled updates are larger, so they jump out of the poor local minima that Adam's smaller, adaptive steps cannot leave
Adam's bias correction acts as hidden weight decay that specifically harms the features vision models learn
SGD noise may favour flatter minima, though flatness is debated; with decoupled weight decay (AdamW) the gap largely closed
SGD keeps BatchNorm running statistics steadier, so its final-epoch gradients are measurably more reliable
explanation: Wilson et al. (2017) found well-tuned SGD + momentum often matched or beat Adam on image classifiers. A popular explanation is that SGD noise favours flatter minima (Keskar et al., 2017), but flatness alone is debated — sharpness can change under a reparametrization that leaves the function unchanged (Dinh et al., 2017). With decoupled weight decay the gap largely closed: Transformers, LLMs and ConvNeXt train with AdamW, while SGD + momentum remains common for ResNet-style CNNs.

q: A gradient g = (3, 4) arrives and you clip by global norm with threshold c = 1. What does the clipped gradient become, and why this rule?
options: (0.6, 0.8): it is rescaled to length c, so its direction is kept and only the step size is capped
(1, 1): each component is capped at c separately, which keeps every coordinate in a safe range
(0, 0): an update whose norm exceeds c is skipped entirely, which protects the weights from a spike
(0.12, 0.16): it is divided by its squared norm, which penalises large gradients more strongly
explanation: If ‖g‖ > c, g ← c·g/‖g‖. Here ‖g‖ = 5, so g becomes (0.6, 0.8): the same direction at length 1. Capping each component separately (1, 1) changes the direction. Clipping guards against exploding gradients in RNNs and Transformers — GPT-3 and Llama 2 clip at 1.0 — but it cannot rescue a gradient that has vanished.

q: You double the batch size of a training run. Which learning-rate adjustment is the recommended starting point?
options: Halve it, because each update in a bigger batch already sums twice as much gradient signal
Raise it: about 2× for SGD (linear rule) or about 1.4× for Adam (square-root rule), then sweep
Leave it as it is and double the epochs, so that the run still takes the same total number of update steps
Leave it as it is and lower the momentum β instead, so the larger velocity does not overshoot
explanation: Larger batches give less noisy gradients (noise falls as 1/√B) but fewer updates per epoch, so each step can be bigger. Goyal et al. (2017) used the linear rule for SGD — ResNet-50 went from 0.1 at batch 256 to 3.2 at 8,192, with warmup; for Adam the square-root rule (about ×1.4) is common. Past a 'critical batch size' the returns diminish, so confirm with a short sweep.

q: Training a large network stalls on a long plateau. Which kind of zero-gradient point is the usual culprit in high dimensions, and why?
options: A bad local minimum far worse than the global one, which traps gradient descent for the rest of training
The global minimum itself, whose basin is so narrow that most initializations overshoot it
A region where every curvature is exactly zero, which only second-order optimizers can cross
A saddle point: a minimum needs every direction to curve upward, about 2⁻ⁿ odds if each were a coin flip
explanation: At a zero-gradient point a minimum needs all n directions to curve upward — about 1 in 1,000 for n = 10 if each were a coin flip, and networks have millions of weights. Dauphin et al. (2014) found that critical points with high training error were saddles. Gradient descent rarely converges to a saddle (Lee et al., 2016) but can crawl near one — the plateau — and momentum and SGD noise help it across. The local minima SGD does find tend to have similar loss, so the goal is a good minimum, not the global one.

q: In PyTorch-style momentum, v ← β·v + ∇J and θ ← θ − α·v, with the usual β = 0.9. What happens when the gradient stays constant for many steps?
options: The velocity decays toward zero, so the step shrinks to almost nothing on a long and consistent slope
The step stays exactly α·∇J, because momentum only changes the direction of each update
The step grows toward α·∇J/(1 − β), 10× larger — β = 0.9 acts like remembering about 10 gradients
The step grows without limit, so momentum always needs gradient clipping to stay stable
explanation: With a steady gradient g the velocity converges to g/(1 − β), so the step becomes α·g/(1 − 0.9) = 10·α·g — acceleration along consistent directions — while directions whose gradient keeps flipping sign cancel out (damped zigzags). Some texts write v ← β·v + (1 − β)·∇J: the same idea with a 10× smaller velocity, so its learning rate is 10× larger.

q: Why does an L1 penalty produce exact zeros while L2 does not, and what does a Lasso solver do to actually land on zero?
options: L1's pull is a constant λ·sign(w) that never fades while L2's pull 2λw shrinks with w; solvers soft-threshold to clip at 0
L2's pull is strongest near zero, so it zeroes more weights; L1 needs an extra clipping step to keep weights alive
L1 spreads its penalty evenly over all weights to smooth predictions; the exact zeros come from early stopping
L2 squares each weight, which removes the small ones first; L1 only removes features once the learning rate decays
explanation: L1 subtracts a fixed amount per step however small w gets; L2 multiplies w by (1 − 2αλ) — geometric decay that never reaches zero. On the penalty alone from 0.100, L1 hits 0 in 10 steps while L2 is still 0.012 after 20. Plain subgradient steps overshoot and jitter near zero (0.011–0.015 left in the chapter's run), so Lasso solvers use soft-thresholding, w ← sign(w)·max(|w| − αλ, 0), which gave exactly 3 zeros on Ch 8's six weights.

q: At inference a BatchNorm layer may see a single example. What does PyTorch use instead of batch statistics, and how are they updated during training?
options: The mean and variance of the very last training batch, saved in the checkpoint and reused unchanged
Running averages updated as running = (1 − m)·running + m·batch, where m = 0.1 weights the new batch
Statistics recomputed over the full validation set after training, for an unbiased population estimate
No statistics at all: γ is reset to 1 and β to 0, so the layer becomes an identity function
explanation: PyTorch's default momentum m = 0.1 is the weight on the NEW batch (it also stores the unbiased variance); Keras defines momentum the other way round — its default 0.99 is the weight on the OLD value. Call model.eval() at test time, or outputs depend on batch-mates. Small batches hurt: the batch mean wobbles by about σ/√B (±71% of σ at B = 2), so below roughly 16–32 per device use GroupNorm or LayerNorm. At inference BatchNorm is a fixed per-channel scale and shift that can be folded into the preceding convolution.

q: With inverted dropout at rate p, surviving activations are multiplied by 1/(1 − p) during training. What is this scaling for?
options: To offset the extra gradient variance that zeroing units adds to each mini-batch update
To stop the surviving neurons from becoming over-confident relative to their temporarily dropped neighbours
To keep dropout consistent with the L2 weight decay applied to the remaining connections
To keep each activation's expected value unchanged, so inference uses every unit with no rescaling
explanation: With p = 0.5, outputs [3, 4, 7, 2, 5] masked to [3, 0, 7, 0, 5] are scaled ×2 to [6, 0, 14, 0, 10]; over many steps neuron 1 averages (6 + 0)/2 = 3, its inference value. At inference every unit is on (model.eval()) and nothing is rescaled. Naming trap: PyTorch's nn.Dropout(p) gives the drop probability, but the original paper (Srivastava et al., 2014) used p for the keep probability.

q: How does early stopping relate to L2 regularization?
options: It is exactly dropout: training time controls how many thinned sub-networks get averaged
It is exactly a max-norm constraint: training halts as soon as any single weight vector grows past a set length
For a quadratic loss with small steps it is approximately L2: fewer steps ≈ larger λ, roughly λ ≈ 1/(2ατ)
It is exactly L1: the number of training steps sets how many weights end at exactly zero
explanation: Bishop (1995) and Goodfellow et al. (§7.8) show that τ gradient steps at learning rate α from near zero act roughly like an L2 penalty of strength λ ≈ 1/(2ατ) — more steps, weaker regularization. It is only approximate (quadratic loss, small steps), and it only works if you restore the best checkpoint (Keras needs restore_best_weights=True). The validation score you stopped on is now optimistic, so report a separate test set.

q: Each random-forest tree trains on a bootstrap sample of N rows. About what share of rows does a given tree never see, and what is that good for?
options: About 36.8%, since (1 − 1/N)ᴺ → e⁻¹; their out-of-bag error can replace a validation set for tuning, but not the test set
About 50%, because a bootstrap deliberately draws half the rows; their error is the final test score you report
About 20%, matching the usual 80/20 split; their error replaces both the validation set and the test set
About 10%, to maximise each tree's training data; those few left-out rows are simply discarded
explanation: A row is missed by one bootstrap with probability (1 − 1/N)ᴺ → e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368, so each tree sees about 63.2% unique rows. Predicting each row only with the trees that never saw it gives the OOB error — close to cross-validation from one fit (Ch 12: OOB accuracy 0.722 vs 5-fold CV 0.726). Use it for tuning, but keep an untouched test set for the number you report. Boosting has no OOB equivalent, so it needs an explicit validation set for early stopping.

q: In XGBoost's regularized objective Ω(f) = γT + ½λΣwⱼ², what does γ control?
options: The size of the leaf weights, pulling every leaf score toward zero so that no single leaf dominates
The price of one more leaf: a split is kept only if its gain exceeds γ
The maximum depth of each tree, capping how many nested questions any tree may ask
The largest absolute leaf weight, enforced as a hard L∞ bound on every tree in the ensemble
explanation: T is the number of leaves, so γ is a complexity cost per leaf — a split whose gain is below γ is pruned (default γ = 0). λ (default 1) is the L2 penalty that shrinks leaf weights, and alpha adds an optional L1 term. Friedman's original gradient boosting has no Ω term; it controls complexity only through depth, shrinkage and subsampling. Split search today uses histogram binning (tree_method='hist', the default since XGBoost 2.0).

q: Each tree in a forest has prediction variance σ² = 1 and the trees are correlated with ρ = 0.9. What does growing from 100 to 1,000 trees do, and what would help more?
options: Variance falls tenfold, from about 0.9 to 0.09, so adding more trees is the main lever to pull here
Variance rises slightly, because more correlated trees amplify the error they share
Variance drops to about zero, since averaging enough trees cancels any kind of error
Almost nothing — the ρσ² = 0.9 floor remains; decorrelating the trees (smaller ρ) helps far more
explanation: Var(average of K trees) = ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/K. With ρ = 0.9, 100 trees give 0.901 and 1,000 give 0.9001: only the second term shrinks. Cutting ρ to 0.3 brings 100 trees to 0.307. That is why random forests add a second layer of randomness — a random feature subset at every split (√M for classification) — so one dominant feature cannot make every tree alike.

q: In round 1 of the chapter's three-house boosting example (squared loss, so g = F − y and h = 1 per row), leaf {A, C} has G = +166.7 and H = 2. What leaf weight does XGBoost's Newton step give with λ = 1?
options: −83.3, the plain mean residual, because λ only matters once the tree is pruned
+83.3, because the leaf weight always takes the sign of the summed gradient G
−55.6, from −G/(H + λ) = −166.7/3, shrunk toward zero from the λ = 0 value of −83.3
−166.7, because the Newton step uses the whole gradient sum G without ever dividing by H
explanation: XGBoost uses second-order (Newton) leaf weights w* = −G/(H + λ), where G and H sum the loss's first and second derivatives over the leaf's rows. At λ = 0 the weight is −166.7/2 = −83.3, the mean residual; at the default λ = 1 it is −166.7/3 = −55.6. The one-row leaf {B} is halved, +166.7 → +83.3: λ shrinks leaves with few rows the most, which is exactly where overfitting lives. (Round 0 starts from F₀ = mean = 333.3, the best constant under squared loss.)

q: In the chapter's 50-layer test, plain sigmoid layers pass back about 4 × 10⁻³² of the gradient, but the same layers with skip connections pass back about 1.09. Why?
options: A residual block y = x + F(x) has ∂y/∂x = 1 + F′(x), so the identity path carries the gradient unshrunk
Skip connections switch the sigmoids to ReLUs internally, so every active slope becomes exactly 1
Skip connections halve the effective depth, so the per-layer shrinkage is applied only 25 times
Skip connections clip the gradient at every layer, which stops it from vanishing or exploding
explanation: The +1 is a path on which the gradient is never shrunk. With a local slope of 0.01 per layer, 50 plain layers pass back 0.01⁵⁰ = 10⁻¹⁰⁰, while 50 residual blocks pass back about 1.01⁵⁰ ≈ 1.64. A sigmoid's slope is at most σ′(0) = 0.25, so 10 plain sigmoid layers keep at most 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁶ from the activations alone. ResNet trained 152 layers this way, and every Transformer block wraps attention and the FFN in residuals (modern LLMs: pre-norm x + F(Norm(x))).

q: Which weight initialization is designed for ReLU layers, and what does it compensate for?
options: Xavier: Var(w) = 2/(n_in + n_out), which averages fan-in and fan-out for tanh or sigmoid layers
He (Kaiming): Var(w) = 2/n_in, doubled because ReLU zeroes about half of its inputs
LeCun: Var(w) = 1/n_in, the scheme built around self-normalizing SELU activations
Orthogonal rows of unit norm, which keep gradient norms fixed only through purely linear layers
explanation: A neuron sums n_in inputs, so Var(z) ≈ n_in·Var(w)·Var(x); ReLU zeroes about half, so He doubles the variance to 2/n_in to keep the signal size steady (std 0.088 for a 256 → 256 layer, vs Xavier's 0.0625). In the chapter's 50-layer run, ReLU with He init kept the gradient near 2.19, std 0.01 killed it (9.3 × 10⁻⁶³) and 1.5 × He exploded it (1.4 × 10⁹). Weights must also be random, not equal, to break symmetry; zero biases are fine.

q: Which statement about activation functions in Transformers matches current practice?
options: Most modern LLMs use plain ReLU in the feed-forward block, because it is the cheapest to compute
GELU's slope is exactly 1 for every positive input, which is why it fixed vanishing gradients in BERT
Transformer hidden layers use sigmoid, because its outputs can be read directly as probabilities
GELU = x·Φ(x), a smooth ReLU, was used in BERT, GPT-2/3 and ViT; Llama-style LLMs use gated SwiGLU
explanation: GELU multiplies x by the standard normal CDF Φ(x): it is smooth, its lowest value is about −0.17 at x ≈ −0.75, and its slope is rarely exactly 0, so units do not die. Most modern LLMs use a gated unit instead — SwiGLU(x) = SiLU(xW₁) ⊙ (xW₂) in Llama, Qwen and DeepSeek, GeGLU in Gemma — with three FFN matrices instead of two. Sigmoid belongs at binary or multi-label outputs and in LSTM gates, not in hidden layers.

q: A ReLU unit outputs zero for every training example and never recovers. What causes this, and what is a typical trigger?
options: Its pre-activation w·x + b is negative for every input, so its gradient is always 0 — often after too high a learning rate
The learning rate is too small, so the updates never push the pre-activation above zero within the training budget
The batch size is too large, which removes the gradient noise that would otherwise push the unit back above zero
The bias started large and positive, which saturates the unit so that no gradient can reach its incoming weights
explanation: When z < 0 for every input, ReLU outputs 0 and passes back 0, so the unit's weights never update. A learning rate that is too high is a common cause (one big step drives the bias very negative). Fixes: a lower learning rate, He initialization, Leaky ReLU or GELU (non-zero slope below 0), or normalization before the activation. ReLU removes only the activation's shrinking — a std-0.01 init still vanishes even with ReLU.

q: Why does scaled dot-product attention divide the scores Q·Kᵀ by √d_k before the softmax?
options: Softmax already normalizes each row to sum to 1, so the division only makes the numbers easier to read
A q·k dot product of unit-variance entries has variance d_k; unscaled, softmax saturates and its gradients vanish
It makes the attention scores independent of the sequence length n, so long inputs cannot swamp the early positions
It reconciles a key size d_k that differs from the value size d_v before the weights are multiplied by V
explanation: q·k sums d_k products, so its spread is √d_k — 8 at d_k = 64. Scores that far apart make softmax nearly one-hot, and the winner's gradient w(1 − w) nearly zero: 0.001 raw vs 0.249 after dividing by 8 in the chapter's program. Without scaling the top weight climbs from 0.52 (d_k = 4) to 0.96 (d_k = 512); with scaling it stays near 0.35. Dividing by d_k instead of √d_k would over-shrink the scores.

q: Why does a Transformer decoder set future attention scores to −∞ before the softmax during training?
options: The future tokens' keys and queries have not been computed yet, so their scores would be undefined
Unmasked future tokens would all get equal weights, wasting capacity on a uniform distribution
The whole target sequence is fed in parallel; without the mask each position could copy the token it must predict
Sinusoidal encodings of later positions carry negative cosines that would distort the softmax sums
explanation: Training feeds the whole sequence at once, so all n next-token predictions come out of one forward pass. The mask puts −∞ above the diagonal before the softmax, so those weights become exactly 0 and each row still sums to 1 — zeroing weights after the softmax would break that. Each position then predicts from earlier tokens only, matching generation; and because a token's keys and values never change, they can be cached (the KV cache).

q: In the cross-attention layer of a Transformer decoder, where do the Query (Q), Key (K) and Value (V) come from?
options: Q from the encoder output; K and V from the decoder's masked self-attention output
Q, K and V all come from the encoder output, so the decoder copies encoder representations
Q and K from the encoder for alignment; V from the decoder to mix in decoder features
Q from the decoder's masked self-attention output; K and V both from the encoder output
explanation: Each decoder token forms a query that searches the encoder's keys and retrieves the encoder's values — this is how an encoder–decoder model (the 2017 translator, T5, BART, Whisper) reads the source sequence. Decoder-only LLMs such as GPT, Gemini and Llama have no cross-attention, only masked self-attention.

q: The original sinusoidal encoding has the property that PE(pos + k) is one fixed linear map (a rotation) of PE(pos), the same for every pos. Why does that matter?
options: A model can learn to attend by relative offset, because shifting by k is the same transformation at any position
It guarantees that position vectors never outweigh token embeddings, so position cannot drown out meaning
It lets models read sequences far longer than in training, which is why sinusoidal encoding extrapolates well
It makes the encodings at different positions exactly orthogonal, so nearby tokens can never be confused
explanation: Each pair of dimensions is a clock hand turning at its own speed, so a shift by k is one fixed rotation — useful for attending by relative position. Extrapolation was the paper's hope, but in practice sinusoidal encoding extrapolates poorly (Press et al., 2022), and learned position embeddings gave nearly identical results in the original paper. Values are bounded in [−1, 1] but not orthogonal. Modern LLMs use RoPE, which rotates q and k so the score itself depends only on the distance.

q: A fraud model has ROC-AUC 0.97, yet investigators say most of its alerts are false. With 0.1% fraud, why is PR-AUC the better number to report?
options: FPR divides false alarms by the huge legitimate class, so thousands of them barely move ROC; precision divides by the alerts raised
PR-AUC is cheaper to compute, because it evaluates one fixed recall level instead of sweeping every threshold
PR-AUC has a random baseline of 0.5 like ROC-AUC, so the two numbers are read on exactly the same scale
ROC-AUC ignores the true positives entirely, while PR-AUC weighs all four confusion-matrix cells equally
explanation: In the chapter's run, 10× more legitimate mail left the FPR at threshold 0.5 unchanged (0.111) — so the ROC curve and its AUC did not move — while precision fell from 0.444 to 0.074. The PR curve ignores true negatives. A random model's PR-AUC equals the positive rate (0.011 when 1.1% are positive), not 0.5. Report PR-AUC as average precision, plus precision@k for the number of alerts the team can review.

q: Detecting a CTR lift from 10% to 11% (α = 0.05, 80% power) needs about 14,100 users per group. Roughly how many would you need to detect a lift of only 0.5 points?
options: About 7,000 per group, because a smaller effect needs proportionally fewer users to detect
About 28,000 per group, because the sample size grows in proportion to 1/δ
About 56,000 per group, because n ≈ 16σ²/δ², so halving δ needs about 4× the users
About 14,100 per group, because the sample size depends only on α and the power
explanation: n per group ≈ 2σ²(z₁₋α/₂ + z₁₋β)²/δ², with σ² = p(1 − p) = 0.09 and (1.96 + 0.84)² ≈ 7.84, so 2 × 0.09 × 7.84/0.01² ≈ 14,100. δ is the minimum detectable effect — the smallest lift worth detecting — and n ∝ 1/δ², so halving it quadruples n (σ² stays about 0.09). Fix n in advance and run in whole weeks; +1 point on 10% is a 10% relative lift, so say which one you mean.

q: An A/B test reads 20 metrics, each at α = 0.05. If the change does nothing, what is the chance of at least one false 'win', and what is the Bonferroni per-metric threshold?
options: About 5%, and α = 0.10, because more metrics add measurement noise that must be allowed for
About 20%, and α = 0.005, using a square-root correction across the whole metric set
About 50%, and α = 0.025, halving α to control the errors between pairs of metrics
About 64%, and α = 0.05/20 = 0.0025, which keeps the family-wise error rate at 5%
explanation: 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 64%. Pre-register one primary metric; for the rest use Bonferroni (α/m = 0.0025) or false-discovery-rate control (Benjamini–Hochberg), which is less conservative. Related traps from the chapter: peeking daily with 10 looks gives about 19% false positives instead of 5%, and a sample-ratio mismatch (50.6% / 49.4% of 10M users, χ² = 1,440) invalidates the result.

q: A model has ROC-AUC 0.92, but among cases it scores 0.97 only 83% are positive, and its scores feed an expected-value calculation (probability × bid). What should you do?
options: Nothing: a ROC-AUC above 0.9 already shows the predicted probabilities are trustworthy
Calibrate on held-out data (Platt, isotonic or temperature scaling); the ranking and its AUC can stay the same
Retrain with balanced class weights, which pulls the over-confident probabilities back down toward the true rates
Lower the decision threshold to 0.83, which turns the raw scores into calibrated probabilities
explanation: AUC measures ranking only; calibration means P(y = 1 | predicted p) = p. Check it with a reliability diagram and the Brier score (predictions 0.9, 0.8, 0.3 on outcomes 1, 0, 0 → ≈ 0.247). Platt and temperature scaling are strictly increasing maps, so they leave the ranking and ROC-AUC unchanged; isotonic regression can create ties. Class weights and resampling make things worse here — they inflate predicted probabilities.

q: You need to explore a 5-million-point embedding set in 2-D and later place tomorrow's new points on the same map. Why might UMAP fit better than scikit-learn's t-SNE?
options: UMAP is deterministic, so every run gives the identical map whatever the random seed
UMAP scales to millions of points and has a transform for new points; scikit-learn's t-SNE has neither
UMAP preserves the true distances between clusters, so its gaps can be read as real separations
UMAP is linear like PCA, so its two output axes are mixtures of the original features that you can interpret
explanation: UMAP runs at about O(n^1.14) on an approximate k-NN graph, scales to millions and places new points with transform. scikit-learn's t-SNE (O(n log n) with Barnes-Hut) slows beyond tens of thousands of points and must be re-run for new data. Both are non-linear and seed-dependent, and gaps mean little in either. UMAP's reputed global-structure edge is mostly its initialization: t-SNE with a PCA start closes most of the gap (Kobak & Linderman, 2021).

q: After PCA you have eigenvalues λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ … ≥ λ_d of the covariance matrix. What fraction of the variance does component i explain?
options: λᵢ²/Σⱼλⱼ², squared to match variance being a second-order quantity
λᵢ/Σⱼλⱼ, because each eigenvalue is the variance of the data along its component
λᵢ − λᵢ₊₁, the variance gained over the next-best component
√λᵢ/Σⱼ√λⱼ, normalized by standard deviations so that components measured in different units compare
explanation: An eigenvalue is the variance along its eigenvector: in the chapter's example the PC1 scores −5.66, −2.83, 0, 2.83, 5.66 have variance 20 = λ₁, and with λ₂ = 0 PC1 explains 20/(20 + 0) = 100%. Keep enough components for 90–95% cumulative variance (PCA(n_components=0.95)), look for the scree elbow, or tune k by validation score when PCA feeds a model. Standardize first, and fit PCA on the training split only.

q: In a t-SNE plot, clusters A and B sit far apart and cluster B looks twice as large as cluster C. What can you safely conclude?
options: A and B are far apart in the original space, because t-SNE keeps large distances intact
B holds about twice as many points as C, because t-SNE preserves the area of each cluster
B is twice as spread out as C in the original space, because t-SNE preserves variances
Little beyond who neighbours whom: t-SNE keeps local neighbourhoods, not gaps or sizes
explanation: t-SNE minimizes KL(P‖Q): tearing real neighbours apart is expensive, but placing distant points at any distance is almost free, so neighbourhoods survive and gaps do not (in Ch 11, clusters 10 and 90 apart came out about equally far apart). Try several perplexity values (default 30) and seeds before trusting a cluster, run PCA to about 50 dimensions first, and never feed t-SNE output to a classifier — there is no transform for new points.

q: Why do distance-based methods such as k-NN weaken when there are many independent, noise-like features?
options: Features with larger units dominate the distance, and that bias grows with every dimension added
High-dimensional vectors no longer fit in memory, so k-d tree indexes fail before any distance is computed at all
Distances concentrate: (D_max − D_min)/D_min → 0, so the nearest and farthest points are almost equally far
The covariance matrix always becomes singular, so no meaningful distance can be defined at all
explanation: For random, independent features the farthest point is barely farther than the nearest (Beyer et al., 1999): in Ch 11's simulation it is about 136× the nearest in 2-D but only 11% farther in 1,000-D. Likewise a ball inside a cube holds 78.5% of a square but 0.25% of a 10-D cube. Real data usually has a low intrinsic dimension and suffers less — which is why reducing dimensions first (PCA) helps.

q: SMOTE makes a synthetic point from minority sample x = [2, 3] and minority neighbour x_nn = [4, 5] with λ = 0.6. What is the new point, and where may SMOTE be applied?
options: [3.2, 4.2], from x + λ(x_nn − x); only inside the training folds, never before the split
[3.0, 4.0], the midpoint; it may be applied to the whole dataset before splitting
[5.2, 6.8], from x_nn + λ·x; it must also be run on the test set to keep ratios equal
[1.2, 1.8], from λ·x; it replaces the original minority rows in both train and test
explanation: x_new = x + λ(x_nn − x) = [2, 3] + 0.6 × [2, 2] = [3.2, 4.2] — a random point on the segment to one of the k = 5 nearest minority neighbours. Resample only the training part of each fold (imbalanced-learn's Pipeline) and keep the test set at the real class ratio; SMOTE before the split puts near-copies of test rows into training. Like class weights, it distorts predicted probabilities, so recalibrate afterwards.

q: You target-encode a 500-value ID column with each category's mean label computed on all training rows, each row included. The labels are coin flips, yet training AUC is 0.78. What happened?
options: The IDs really do carry signal; the model found a genuine pattern that the test set will confirm
Each row's encoding contains its own label; out-of-fold encoding gives the honest AUC of about 0.50
The encoding imposed an order on the IDs; switching to one-hot encoding will remove the effect
The encoding was not smoothed; adding smoothing with m = 10 on its own will bring the AUC back to about 0.50
explanation: With about 4 rows per ID, a category's 'mean' is mostly that row's own label, so the feature copies the answer. In the chapter's run, in-sample encoding scored 0.778, smoothing alone barely helped (0.771), and out-of-fold encoding — each row encoded only from the other folds — gave 0.502, matching the test rows (0.506). scikit-learn's TargetEncoder (1.3+) cross-fits automatically; CatBoost's ordered target statistics are the same idea.

q: High earners deliberately skip a survey's income question. What kind of missingness is this, and what is the main defence?
options: MCAR: the gaps are pure chance, so dropping the incomplete rows gives unbiased results
MAR: the gaps depend on other observed columns, so KNN imputation from those columns fixes it fully
Not missing data at all: a skipped income answer is best encoded as an income of zero
MNAR: missingness depends on the missing value itself; add an is_missing flag and find out why
explanation: MCAR = pure chance; MAR = depends on columns you can see (older people skip more often); MNAR = depends on the value itself (high earners skip because income is high). No imputation fully fixes MNAR — add the flag so the model can learn that missingness is informative, and investigate the cause. Under MAR, mean-filling is biased and shrinks the column (std 15.1 → 11.7 in the chapter's demo), while KNN imputation does much better.

q: You predict a store's sales for day t with a 7-day rolling-average feature, and the label is known immediately. Which feature definition and validation split are leak-free?
options: mean(sales[t−7 … t]) with a random 80/20 split, so both sets see every season
mean(sales[t−3 … t+3]), a centred window, validated with a time-based split
mean(sales[t−7 … t−1]) — shift by one before rolling — with a split by time
mean(sales[t−7 … t]) with back-filled gaps, validated by shuffled K-fold
explanation: Every feature must already exist at the moment you predict: t_known(x) ≤ t_predict. A window that includes day t contains the target; a centred window peeks 3 days ahead; back-fill copies future values into the past; random or shuffled splits train on Friday to predict Wednesday. Use .shift(1).rolling(7), split by time (TimeSeriesSplit), forward-fill only, and leave a gap equal to the label delay when labels arrive late (fraud chargebacks: 30–90 days).

q: When designing Gmail's spam filter, which offline evaluation target best matches the product's costs?
options: Recall at a fixed, very low false-positive rate, plus PR-AUC — a real email lost in spam is the costly error
Overall accuracy, because spam is common enough in email that accuracy cannot be misleading here
Maximum recall at any false-positive rate, because letting one spam email through is the worst error
ROC-AUC alone, because it is threshold-free and so needs no business costs to interpret it
explanation: A legitimate email sent to spam is the expensive mistake, so you fix a very low false-positive rate and maximize the spam caught under that constraint, reporting PR-AUC as well. Online, an A/B test tracks the false-positive rate through users' 'Not spam' clicks. Google reports that its RETVec text vectorizer raised Gmail's spam detection rate by 38% and cut false positives by 19.4% (Nov 2023).

q: What does a feature store with point-in-time joins give an ML system?
options: Versioned model checkpoints, so a bad deployment can be rolled back and traffic split between versions
One feature definition for training (offline) and serving (online), with training rows seeing only values known at event time
A cache of raw inputs next to the model server, which removes database round-trips from online inference
Cached feature statistics that speed up Bayesian hyperparameter search across concurrent experiments
explanation: Training-serving skew — a feature computed one way in a batch job and another way per request — is the #1 cause of 'great offline, terrible live'. A feature store keeps one definition, with an offline store (BigQuery, S3) for training and an online store (Redis, Bigtable) for serving; a point-in-time join gives each training example the latest value with timestamp ≤ its event time. On Google Cloud this is the Agent Platform Feature Store in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), as of Nov 2026; Feast is the common open-source choice. Still monitor: stale or missing values cause skew too.

q: PSI against training data scores 0.18 for session length after an app redesign, and jumps to 8.3 for a duration feature the morning after a serving release. How should you read these?
options: Both are stable, because PSI only signals real trouble once it passes 10
Each calls for immediate retraining, since any PSI over 0.1 means real drift
The 0.18 needs a rollback, while the 8.3 is seasonal drift that will settle
0.18 is in the watch band (0.1–0.25); 8.3 overnight points to a skew bug, such as a units change
explanation: PSI = Σ (aᵢ − eᵢ)·ln(aᵢ/eᵢ) over 10 training-decile bins; rules of thumb: under 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 watch, over 0.25 act. In the chapter's run, sessions +30% scored 0.178 and +50% scored 0.425, while serving seconds instead of minutes scored 8.283 — skew looks like an enormous overnight 'drift'. Retrain on sustained drift (e.g. PSI > 0.25 for days, not a one-day blip) or a metric drop, and ship each new model via offline eval → shadow → canary → ramp with auto-rollback.

q: How does Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) build its vocabulary?
options: It splits words at morphological boundaries taken from language-specific dictionaries of prefixes and suffixes
It scores every possible segmentation by likelihood and keeps the best one using dynamic programming
It starts from characters or bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair until the target size
It cuts text into fixed 4-character windows and gives each distinct window its own integer ID
explanation: BPE counts adjacent symbol pairs, merges the most frequent into a new token, records the merge and repeats; new text is encoded by replaying the merges in order. Byte-level BPE (GPT-2 onward, Llama 3) starts from the 256 byte values, so no string is out-of-vocabulary. WordPiece (BERT) merges by a likelihood score count(ab)/(count(a)·count(b)); Unigram LM (T5) starts large and prunes. Vocabularies run from 32,000 (Llama 2) to about 262K (Gemma 3).

q: How does RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding), used in Llama, Gemma, Qwen and Mistral, encode position?
options: It rotates each pair of q and k numbers by position × θᵢ, so the score q·k depends only on the offset n − m
It adds a position-dependent bias inside every feed-forward block, separating position from attention
It looks up a learned vector for each position and adds it to the input embedding, as BERT and GPT-2 do
It masks value vectors outside a fixed radius, so each token only attends within a sliding window
explanation: (R_m q)·(R_n k) = q·R_(n−m) k: rotating both vectors by their own positions leaves a score that depends only on the distance; it is applied to Q and K (not V) in every layer, with no added parameters. RoPE does not extrapolate for free — a model trained on 8K tokens has never seen the angles for position 30,000 — so long-context models rescale it (Position Interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN; Llama 3 uses base 500,000).

q: MQA and GQA both shrink the KV cache. What is the structural difference between them?
options: GQA keeps more value heads than key heads; MQA keeps an equal number of each, both set to one
GQA groups query heads by layer depth; MQA groups them by the patterns each head has learned
MQA shares one K/V head across all h query heads; GQA shares g K/V heads, each serving h/g query heads
GQA applies rotary embeddings only to the keys to save memory; MQA applies them to both keys and queries
explanation: MHA has h K/V heads, GQA g (1 < g < h), MQA one. For a Llama-2/3-70B-sized model (80 layers, 64 query heads, head size 128, FP16) the cache is 2.5 MiB per token with MHA, 320 KiB with GQA-8 and 40 KiB with MQA — 10 GiB vs 1.25 GiB at 4K tokens for MHA vs GQA. GQA keeps quality near MHA (Llama 2 70B, Llama 3, Mistral 7B, Gemma 2/3); MQA (PaLM, Falcon-7B) saves the most but can lose a little quality. MLA (DeepSeek-V2/V3) caches a 576-number latent instead.

q: A common misconception is that FlashAttention approximates attention. Which description is correct?
options: It replaces softmax with a kernel feature map, trading a little accuracy for linear memory and compute
It attends only to a local window plus a few global tokens, which makes attention linear in length
It stores attention weights in INT8 and rebuilds FP16 values in the backward pass, halving memory
It is exact: it works in SRAM tiles with an online softmax and never writes the n × n matrix to HBM
explanation: FlashAttention loads Q, K and V tiles into fast on-chip SRAM, keeps a running max and sum (online softmax) and writes each output row once, so the n × n score matrix — 20 GB per head per layer at n = 100K in FP16 — is never stored. The result is the same up to floating-point rounding; memory drops to O(n), compute stays O(n²), and it runs faster because attention is limited by memory traffic. Linear attention, sliding windows and sparse patterns are the approximate alternatives.

q: Mixtral 8x7B routes each token to the top 2 of 8 expert FFNs. Which statement about its cost is correct?
options: It stores 56B parameters and runs 14B per token, since all eight 7B experts are full copies
It stores 46.7B parameters but runs about 12.9B per token: MoE saves compute, not memory
It stores and runs only 12.9B per token, because idle experts are loaded from disk on demand
It runs all 46.7B per token, because top-2 routing evaluates every expert before choosing two
explanation: Only the feed-forward blocks are copied into experts; attention and embeddings are shared, so '8x7B' stores 46.7B and runs 12.9B (28%) per token — yet every expert must stay in memory. Left alone, routing collapses onto a few experts, so Switch Transformer added a load-balancing loss (at its minimum, α, under uniform routing); DeepSeek-V3 uses bias-based balancing and picks 8 of 256 experts plus a shared one. Switch Transformer itself routes each token to just one expert.

q: Which statement about the KV cache in autoregressive generation is correct?
options: It stores past tokens' K and V, cutting K/V work from O(n²) to O(n) per generation; each step still attends to all n cached keys
It makes every new token cost O(1), because attention then only needs to read the newest key and value pair
It speeds up training as well, because activations are cached between epochs instead of being recomputed
It stores the n × n attention weights, so the softmax never has to be recomputed for earlier tokens
explanation: Thanks to the causal mask a token's K and V never change, so recomputing them every step (1 + 2 + … + n = O(n²)) is waste; with the cache each step computes K and V for the new token only. The query is still compared with all t cached keys, so attention over n steps stays O(n²), and decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound. The price is memory: 2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes — 320 KiB per token for Llama-2/3-70B in FP16. It does not speed up training.

q: Why do Transformer and LLM recipes use AdamW instead of Adam with an L2 penalty added to the loss?
options: AdamW drops bias correction, which removes the oversized first steps that Adam + L2 suffers from
AdamW keeps one optimizer number per weight instead of two, halving the memory of Adam + L2
AdamW applies the L2 term before the gradient is computed, so the loss surface itself becomes smoother to descend
Adam divides the L2 gradient by √v̂, so weights with large gradients barely decay; AdamW decays weights directly
explanation: Adding λθ to the gradient is exact weight decay only under plain SGD. Under Adam the sum is divided by √v̂, so the decay depends on gradient history: in Ch 16's 2,000-step simulation Adam + L2 left weights at 0.023, 0.830 or 1.012 for quiet, medium or loud gradients, while AdamW left all three at 0.830. AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) updates θ ← θ − α(m̂/(√v̂ + ε) + λθ). Llama 2's recipe: β₂ = 0.95, weight decay 0.1, clipping at 1.0, 2,000 warmup steps, cosine decay to 10% of peak. AdamW still keeps two numbers per weight; Lion keeps one.

q: What is the pre-training objective of decoder-only LLMs such as GPT, Gemini and Llama?
options: Masked-token cross-entropy: hide 15% of tokens and predict them from context on both sides, as BERT does
A contrastive loss that pulls in-context example pairs together and pushes random negatives apart
Mean squared error between the model's hidden states and the embeddings of a frozen teacher encoder
Next-token cross-entropy, L = −(1/T)·Σₜ log p(xₜ | x<ₜ), predicting each token from its left context
explanation: A causal mask hides the future, so one T-token sequence gives T training examples in a single forward pass, and no labels are needed. BERT's masked-LM loss uses only the 15% of tokens it masks, while a decoder gets a next-token loss at 100% of positions — one reason next-token prediction scales so well. Example: true-token probabilities 0.30, 0.20, 0.50, 0.10 give L = 1.452 nats, perplexity ≈ 4.27.

q: In supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on chat data, which tokens does the training loss cover?
options: Every token of the conversation — system prompt, user turns and assistant replies — weighted equally
Only the first token of each assistant reply, so that the model learns how good answers begin
Only the assistant's reply tokens, including the end-of-turn token; the prompt is read but masked out
A random half of the assistant tokens in each batch, like masked language modelling without replacement
explanation: L_SFT = −(1/|R|)·Σ log p(xₜ | x<ₜ) over the reply tokens R; prompt labels are set to −100 in PyTorch / Hugging Face. Scoring the end-of-turn token teaches the model to stop. SFT needs thousands to about a million examples: InstructGPT used about 13K human demonstrations, and LIMA's 1,000 curated examples showed SFT mostly teaches style — knowledge comes from pre-training. SFT cannot learn that answer A beats answer B, which is why preference tuning follows.

q: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) reaches the same goal as RLHF while removing a component. Which one?
options: The separately trained reward model and the RL loop: it trains on preference pairs, using β·log(π_θ/π_ref) as an implicit reward
The frozen reference model π_ref: it optimizes the preference labels directly, with no reference anywhere in its loss
Human preference data: it generates its own preference labels through self-critique, just as Constitutional AI does
The KL constraint: it maximizes raw preference probabilities with no pull at all back toward the SFT model
explanation: The RLHF objective has a closed-form best policy, so the reward can be written β·log(π*/π_ref) + β·log Z(x); in the Bradley–Terry loss β·log Z(x) cancels, giving L_DPO = −log σ(β·[(log π_θ(y_w) − log π_ref(y_w)) − (log π_θ(y_l) − log π_ref(y_l))]). The frozen reference IS still used (SimPO and ORPO drop it). Worked example, β = 0.1: a margin of 0.4 lowers the loss from ln 2 = 0.693 to 0.513.

q: GRPO removes PPO's value network (critic). How does it get a baseline for the advantage?
options: It uses the running mean reward over all previous training steps as one global baseline
It samples G answers per prompt and scores each against its own group: Aᵢ = (rᵢ − mean)/std
It uses the frozen SFT model's log-probabilities as a stand-in for the learned value of each state
It trains a small discriminator that predicts whether a response is above or below average
explanation: Every token of answer i gets Âᵢ = (rᵢ − mean(r₁…r_G))/(std + ε); R1-Zero used G = 16. With 3 of 8 answers correct, mean 0.375 and std 0.484 give +1.29 to each correct answer and −0.77 to each wrong one. No critic roughly halves PPO's training state. A group that is all right or all wrong has zero advantages and teaches nothing, so recipes keep prompts of medium difficulty.

q: What did the Chinchilla scaling study (Hoffmann et al., 2022) conclude about spending a fixed training-compute budget?
options: Model size should grow with the cube root of compute, favouring very big models on small, curated datasets
Every model should train on a fixed 300B tokens, the amount that proved enough at every size studied
Parameters matter more than data at scale, so extra compute should mostly buy a bigger model
Parameters and tokens should grow together, about 20 tokens per parameter — a 70B model on ~1.4T tokens
explanation: With C ≈ 6·N·D and D ≈ 20·N, N_opt = √(C/120): a 10²² FLOPs budget gives about 9.1B parameters on 183B tokens. Kaplan's earlier fit (N ∝ C^0.73) favoured size, which is why GPT-3 had 175B parameters on only 300B tokens. Chinchilla (70B, 1.4T tokens) beat Gopher (280B, 300B tokens) on a similar budget. The 20× rule is optimal for training compute only; models that will serve heavily are over-trained (Llama 3 8B: about 1,875 tokens per parameter).

q: Why do Transformers use LayerNorm or RMSNorm rather than BatchNorm?
options: They normalize each token over its own features, so training and inference match at any batch size, padding or one-token generation
BatchNorm cannot be folded into a neighbouring matrix multiply, which makes it too slow inside attention layers
LayerNorm and RMSNorm regularize more strongly, because their per-token statistics inject extra noise
BatchNorm has no learned scale and shift, so the network can never undo the normalization when it hurts
explanation: BatchNorm averages one feature across the batch, which mixes positions and padding, fluctuates strongly in NLP (Shen et al., PowerNorm, 2020) and needs running averages that differ from training. LayerNorm normalizes each token (x = [3.0, 1.5, 2.0] → [1.34, −1.07, −0.27]); RMSNorm skips the mean and β (RMS 2.25 → [1.33, 0.67, 0.89]) — one reduction instead of two — and sits before each block (pre-norm) in Llama, Gemma, Mistral, Qwen and DeepSeek. With no batch noise, they are not regularizers.

q: A fraud model is trained on 9,900 legitimate and 100 fraud rows. In what order should you work through the imbalance fixes?
options: SMOTE on the full dataset first, then class weights, then choose the threshold on the test set
Undersample the majority class to 50/50, then judge the model by accuracy on a balanced test set
Honest metrics (PR-AUC, recall), then the threshold, then class weights, then resample training folds only, then recalibrate
Class weights first, then resampling, keeping the default 0.5 threshold so the probabilities stay calibrated
explanation: Cheapest first. Moving the threshold is free: t* = C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN) = 0.1 when a miss costs 9× a false alarm, and in the chapter it lifted recall from 0.28 to 0.61. Balanced weights w_c = n/(K·n_c) give fraud 50 and legit ≈ 0.505. Thresholds and weights only move the operating point — PR-AUC stayed 0.45. Resample (SMOTE, undersampling) last and only inside training folds; weights and resampling inflate predicted probabilities, so recalibrate.

q: Your tree ensemble ranks user_id as its most important feature by the default impurity (MDI) importance. What should you check next, and with what?
options: Nothing: impurity importance is measured on held-out data, so a high-cardinality ID column cannot fool it
Permutation importance on held-out data — model-agnostic: shuffle one column and measure the score drop
L1 regularization as an embedded filter, since impurity and permutation importance always agree
SHAP values read as causal effects, which prove whether user_id truly drives the outcome
explanation: MDI sums impurity drops on training data and is biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features: in Ch 12 a random ID scored MDI 0.439 but permutation importance only +0.018. Permutation importance is model-agnostic and computed after training on held-out data; its pitfall is that correlated features share credit. SHAP explains individual predictions but is not causal. Then drop the ID — it also invites leakage.

q: Speculative decoding lets a fast draft model propose K tokens that the target model verifies in one forward pass. With the standard accept/resample rule, what is guaranteed about output quality?
options: Quality drops in proportion to how often drafts are rejected, so a weak draft model hurts the answers
It is slightly lossy: the target accepts some near-miss tokens to keep throughput high
Quality improves, because rejected tokens are resampled from a corrected, sharper distribution
It is provably lossless: the output follows the target model's distribution exactly
explanation: Each draft token xᵢ is kept with probability min(1, p(xᵢ)/q(xᵢ)), with p the target's and q the draft's probability; the first rejection is resampled from max(0, p − q) renormalized, and if all K survive the target adds a bonus token. Expected tokens per target pass: (1 − α^(K+1))/(1 − α) — 4.10 at α = 0.9, K = 4 — about 2–3× faster in practice. Gains vanish when acceptance collapses, e.g. for creative high-temperature text.

q: A video app must pick about 25 items from 800M videos for each user within a ~300 ms page budget. Which design fits?
options: Score all 800M videos with the heavy ranking model on every request, using bigger accelerators
Precompute one global top-25 list each night and serve the same list to every user next day
Two-tower retrieval with ANN search (800M → ~1,000), a heavier multi-task ranker (→ ~100), then re-ranking
One LLM prompt per request that lists the whole 800M-video catalogue and asks the model to choose 25 of them
explanation: Scoring 800M × 128-dim embeddings exactly costs ≈ 1.0 × 10¹¹ multiply-adds per request. In a two-tower model the item vectors are precomputed and score = u·v, so retrieval is a nearest-neighbour search (~10 ms). The ranker (Wide & Deep, DCN-v2; heads such as P(click) and expected watch time) adds rich user × item crosses on ~1,000 candidates (~20 ms); re-ranking handles diversity, freshness and safety (~10 ms). Stable parts are precomputed, but each request is scored live.

q: Why does production RAG usually combine BM25 keyword search with dense vector retrieval?
options: Vectors catch paraphrases but blur exact tokens such as error codes and product IDs; BM25 matches them — fuse with RRF
Averaging any two ranking signals always beats one, whatever the query type, the domain or the term rarity
BM25 is much faster than vector search, so the hybrid mainly cuts latency rather than improving recall
BM25 can index documents newer than the embedding model's training cutoff, which vectors cannot find
explanation: BM25 catches exact tokens that embeddings blur (an error code like E-4012, product codes, names); vectors catch paraphrases. Fuse the two rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (k = 60) — ranks, not raw scores, so BM25's bigger numbers cannot decide alone. Then retrieve about 50, rerank with a cross-encoder, keep 3–10, and filter by the user's permissions at retrieval time.

q: In Liu et al.'s 'Lost in the Middle' study (20 passages, one containing the answer), how did GPT-3.5-Turbo's accuracy depend on where the answer passage sat?
options: Almost flat — about 75% wherever the passage was, so its position barely matters
U-shaped: 75.8% first, 53.8% at position 10 (below its 56.1% with no passages), 63.2% last
Steadily rising toward the end, because the most recent tokens always dominate attention
Near zero in the middle, because models ignore every passage except the first and last two
explanation: Best at the start (primacy), second-best at the end (recency), worst in the middle — where the passages actually hurt compared with answering closed-book. The 16K-context version scored almost the same, so a bigger window did not help; Claude-1.3's dip was only about 4 points. For RAG: rerank and send fewer chunks, put the best chunk first and the runner-up last, and put the question after the documents. The effect is weaker today but not gone — measure it on your own task.

q: How do reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1 differ from a standard LLM prompted to 'think step by step'?
options: They use far larger context windows, so more intermediate steps can be stored before the answer
They are fine-tuned only on expert-written chain-of-thought traces, with no reinforcement learning stage at all
They run Monte Carlo tree search at inference, branching on uncertainty before they commit
They are trained with RL on checkable rewards, so long reasoning and self-checking emerge from training
explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting is an inference-time trick for any model. DeepSeek-R1-Zero applied GRPO with rule-based rewards (a correct final answer, reasoning inside think tags) straight to the base model with no SFT; longer thinking and 'Wait…' self-checks emerged, and AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 77.9%. The released R1 added cold-start SFT, more RL and about 800K rejection-sampled SFT examples for readability. OpenAI's o-series also uses large-scale RL, but its recipe is unpublished.
